summary: LunarWindow is a web app that shows mission planners when a landing site at the lunar south pole can both generate power and talk to Earth. At the pole, the Sun skims the horizon and Earth bobs up and down, so a good place can be a bad time. At one site, Earth is visible 95% of the time in late November and 0% two weeks later. You pick a real south-pole site and a date range, see the Sun and Earth from the lander’s point of view, and get the hours when both are visible together. You can compare plans, find the best window, or test what happens if the launch slips. The app combines NASA JPL Horizons ephemerides with NASA LOLA terrain elevation data. Real terrain matters: at one site it cuts the longest joint window by 74% compared with a flat horizon. Every source is archived, checksummed and labelled, so planners, payload teams and educators can screen sites quickly and check each result.

Suggested Detailed Project Description:

What it does and how it works
LunarWindow answers a question every lunar south-pole mission has to ask: when will a site have sunlight for power and a direct line of sight to Earth for communication, at the same time? At the pole, the Sun circles the sky within about 1.5° of the horizon, and Earth bobs by up to about 6.7° because of libration. A site that works well one week can lose all contact with Earth two weeks later.

You pick one of three verified south-pole reference sites (Connecting ridge, Shackleton inner wall or Malapert massif) and a date range. The app then shows the sky from the lander’s point of view, with the Sun and Earth moving over the real terrain horizon. A timeline marks every hour when the Sun is up, Earth is up, or both are. From there you can:

  • compare two plans side by side,
  • list every joint Sun-and-Earth window above a chosen length,
  • run a launch-slip test that shifts the dates by 7 or 30 days.

Behind the scenes, the backend takes hourly Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL Horizons, with the observer placed on the Moon. It builds a terrain horizon from NASA LOLA elevation models at 5 m, 20 m and 120 m resolution, tracing 3,600 rays out to 200 km. It then calculates visibility for every hour and turns that into metrics, windows and countdowns.

Benefits and intended impact
Terrain changes the answer a lot. At Connecting ridge, a flat horizon promises Sun and Earth together 43% of the month, with a longest window of 312 hours. With NASA’s real terrain, that drops to 11% and 81 hours. LunarWindow makes that difference visible in seconds and shows why a window opens or closes, not just a percentage.

It’s built for early-stage comparisons by lander companies, agencies, payload and rover teams, and educators. It isn’t meant for automated site certification.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python with FastAPI
  • Frontend: Next.js, React and TypeScript
  • Deployment: Docker
  • Data: NASA JPL Horizons ephemerides and NASA LOLA elevation models from NASA Goddard’s PGDA
  • Cross-checks: LROC QuickMap

The demo runs offline from an archived, SHA-256-checksummed data release, so it doesn’t depend on live API calls.

Creativity
Existing tools such as JPL Horizons, Moon Trek, QuickMap and Ohio University’s Lunar Planner are powerful, but they cover different parts of the problem. LunarWindow puts them together around a single decision: the joint Sun-and-Earth window for your site and your dates. It pairs the lander’s-eye sky view with the timeline so planners can see the geometry, not just read numbers.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty. Every source is archived and checksummed, and every model and assumption is labelled in the app. Event times are bracketed by the hourly sampling.
  • Validation. Our Sun and Earth angles agree with LROC QuickMap to within 0.005°, and an independent recomputation of the terrain horizon matches to 0.0001°.
  • Known limits. Only one site’s terrain horizon (Connecting ridge) has been fully reviewed, and the others are still preliminary. Power generation, antenna link budgets and relays aren’t modelled yet. The three reference sites are reference points, not landing recommendations.
